title: Diners: The Most American Establishment?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of the American diner: its origins in 1870s-1890s horse-drawn lunch wagons (Walter Scott of Providence, Sam Jones and the Owl wagon, Charles Palmer's 1891 patent), the prefab diner manufacturers (Worcester Lunch Car and Carriage Company, Jerry O'Mahony Company, P.J. Tierney Company), the train-car styling that gave diners their name, the Greek immigrant domination of diner ownership, post-World War II suburban expansion and changes like servers and chrome/neon looks, Southern diner analogues and chains like Waffle House, Denny's and IHOP, the rise of fast food, diners in politics (Red Arrow Diner, Jimmy Carter, Bill Clinton), diners in pop culture (Nighthawks, the movie Diner, Tarantino, Twin Peaks' Double R Diner, Seinfeld, Suzanne Vega's song), and New Jersey's concentration of diners. The episode closes with listener mail from Sheila of Decatur, Georgia, about why men's and women's buttons are on opposite sides.

entities.name: Worcester Lunch Car and Carriage Manufacturing Company

segments.title: Opening banter and tour dates
segments.summary: Josh plugs upcoming Pacific Northwest tour dates. Chuck shares news about the loss of their dog Charlie and thanks listeners, and the hosts transition to the diner topic.

segments.title: Introduction to the Moran Square Diner
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode's topic and thank Livia, whose sibling-in-law Ember runs the Moran Square Diner in Fitchburg, Massachusetts, which restored Worcester Lunch Car No. 765 from 1939.

segments.title: Lunch wagons origins
segments.summary: Walter Scott of Providence, Rhode Island, sold food from a horse-drawn wagon to late-shift workers. Sam Jones copied the idea with a late-night wagon called the Owl, then added a kitchen and counter in 1887 and expanded to Springfield.

segments.title: Patents and prefab diner manufacturers
segments.summary: Charles Palmer bought Sam Jones's setup and patented a design with a counter and service windows in 1891. Manufacturers including the Worcester Lunch Car and Carriage Company, Jerry O'Mahony Company, and P.J. Tierney Company built prefab diners that were durable and still in use.

segments.title: Stationary diners and railroad car look
segments.summary: Lunch wagons were parked in one place, and in 1913 manufacturers began making stationary, twenty-six-foot diners. Diners were shaped like railroad dining cars, which explains the name. Art Deco chrome and features like Casey's Diner in Natick and Mickey's Diner in Saint Paul are discussed, and the hosts debate whether trains or ships inspired the streamline look.

segments.title: Greek immigrant diner owners
segments.summary: Diners in the early days were a working-class place and generally owned by European immigrants. Greek immigrants, many from the island of Carpathos, came to own roughly ninety percent of US diners, often running family businesses. Josh offers anecdotal Atlanta examples and notes Greek-style pastries on diner menus.

segments.title: Post-WWII suburban diners and women workers
segments.summary: After World War II, the wartime economic boom and suburban growth gave diners new middle-class customers. Working women who stayed in the workforce wanted to eat out, and diners added table service and female servers, appealing to families. Diners added windows, pastel colors, mirrored ceilings, and neon Googie signs in the 1950s.

segments.title: Southern diners and the Yankee label
segments.summary: Diner culture was more Northeastern. In the South, diner-like places existed but were not called diners, which the hosts link to Waffle House (opened 1955) and Silver Skillet.

segments.title: Chains, fast food, and diner revival
segments.summary: Waffle House, Denny's (1953) and IHOP (1958) became diner-style chains. Fast food also competed with local diners. Nostalgia of the 1970s, such as Happy Days and Grease, helped revive diners.

segments.title: Waffle House discussion and break
segments.summary: Hosts discuss their personal Waffle House experiences, Waffle House Index used by FEMA, and then take a break.

segments.title: Diners in politics
segments.summary: Diners have long been places where politicians meet voters. The Red Arrow Diner in Manchester, New Hampshire, became a campaign tradition after Bill Clinton's 1992 push. Jimmy Carter earlier visited the Chat and Chew diner.

segments.title: Diners in pop culture
segments.summary: Edward Hopper's Nighthawks, Barry Levinson's movie Diner, and Tarantino's diner scenes are discussed. Twin Peaks' Double R Diner was filmed at the Mar-T Cafe in North Bend, Washington. Tom's Diner on Broadway in Manhattan inspired a Seinfeld establishing shot and a Suzanne Vega song.

segments.title: New Jersey diners
segments.summary: New Jersey has the most diners, about 600 of roughly 2,000 nationwide according to Smithsonian Magazine. The Sopranos is cited as showing diner culture there.

segments.title: Listener mail: button placement
segments.summary: Sheila of Decatur, Georgia, explains that men's and women's clothing buttons are on opposite sides because upper-class women were dressed by assistants, and most people are right-handed.
